1.sense: A question that works as a reminder, put to one man. It asks him to look back at something already done for him before it asks anything at all of him.

notes.t: Sharh is the word for opening a thing out flat so that what is inside becomes reachable, which is why a commentary written on a book is called a sharh.
The question form, have We not, is used because the answer is not in doubt. Arabic uses this shape to make the listener supply the yes himself rather than be told it.

That the chest of the Prophet ﷺ was opened physically, once as a child and again on the night of the Ascension, is narrated in the Sahih collections. Whether this verse points at that event, or at the widening of the heart to carry the message, or at both, is where the commentators divide.
notes.src: the opening of the chest is narrated from Anas ibn Malik in Sahih Muslim, Book of Faith; the application to this verse is the disputed part

links.why: Musa asks for exactly this, my Lord expand for me my chest
whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his chest for Islam

2.sense: The second thing is a weight lifted off. The verse does not say what the weight was, and the verse after it says only what the weight was doing to him.

notes.t: Wizr is a load carried on the back, from the same root as wazir, the minister who carries a share of the ruler's load. It is a word for freight, not for guilt in itself.

What this burden was is read several ways: the weight of the years before revelation came, the strain of carrying the mission, or the distress at the state of his people. The Qur'an does not name it here.
notes.src: at-Tabari and later commentators set out these readings without agreeing on one

links.why: that Allah may forgive you what preceded and what followed
the surah before this one, listing what was already done for him

3.sense: The load is described by the sound it made. Anqada is the noise of something under strain, the creak of a joint or a beam at the point of giving way.

notes.t: Naqid is the sound a saddle or a bone makes when it is loaded past what it can hold. The verse picks a sound rather than a weight to say how heavy the burden was, which is more exact than any number would be.
The clause is subordinate, so the sentence is still about the removal announced in the verse before. The description of the load only arrives once we have been told it is gone.

links.why: the burden this clause is attached to and describing
We know your chest is straitened by what they say

4.sense: The third thing is not internal. The first two happened inside him; this one happened in the mouths of other people, and it was stated while most of those people were still against him.

notes.t: Dhikr is mention, being spoken of. The promise that the name would be raised was made in a town where that same name was being used as an insult in the street outside.
The declaration of faith joins his name to the name of Allah, and the call to prayer says both of them aloud five times a day wherever Muslims settle. The verse is commonly read as describing this.

A report is transmitted in which Allah says that whenever He is mentioned His Messenger is mentioned with Him. The chain is graded differently by different scholars, and the point it makes is audible in the adhan without it.
notes.src: reported from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and cited by Ibn Kathir on this verse; the chain is assessed differently by different scholars

links.why: Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ
He sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among themselves

5.sense: The three reminders end and a rule follows from them. The word is with, not after. The ease is not placed at the far end of the hardship but alongside it, inside the same stretch of time.

notes.t: Maa in Arabic is accompaniment. The language had a plain word for after, bada, and the Qur'an uses it elsewhere for this very subject. Here it did not use it.
Al-usr carries the definite article and yusran does not. The exegetes read this as one known hardship set against an unspecified ease, which is what makes the repetition in the next verse do work.
The rule is given to a man who has just been reminded of three specific things already done for him, so it is presented as an inference from his own record rather than as a general saying.

links.why: Allah will bring about ease after hardship, the same promise worded with after
Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can carry

6.sense: The same sentence again, one word lighter at the front. Nothing new is added, and that is the substance of it: the statement is repeated rather than developed, and the repeating is itself the reassurance.

notes.t: Because al-usr is definite in both verses, Arabic grammar takes the second mention to be the same hardship. Because yusran is indefinite in both, the two eases are read as two different ones.

The saying that one hardship will never overcome two eases is widely quoted. It is transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ in incomplete form and also as a statement of companions and of al-Hasan al-Basri, and the scholars hold it more confidently as the latter.
notes.src: reported in mursal form by at-Tabari and attributed to Ibn Masʿud and to al-Hasan al-Basri in the commentaries

notes.t: Saying a thing twice in Arabic is emphasis, not padding, and the same device stands at the head of Al-Fatiha where the two names of mercy are said and then said again.

links.why: the identical sentence one verse earlier
do not weaken and do not grieve, spoken after a defeat

7.sense: The instruction says what to do with the ease when it comes. Finishing one thing is not the start of rest, it is the start of the next exertion.

notes.t: Nasab is effort that tires the body. The command is not simply to work but to spend yourself, and it is the same root the Qur'an uses in the negative of the people of the Garden, whom no fatigue will touch.

What the finishing and the labouring refer to is read variously: finishing the prayer and then supplicating, finishing the conveying of the message and then standing in worship, finishing worldly work and then turning to devotion. The wording is left general.
notes.src: at-Tabari lists the sayings of the early exegetes and the wording carries more than one of them

notes.t: The verse arrives immediately after two promises of ease, which places the command exactly where a person would expect to be told to stop.

links.why: you have a long stretch of occupation by day, so remember the name of your Lord
and worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you

8.sense: The last words aim the effort. Work until you are tired, and then want nothing out of it except Him. The surah closes on the same address it has used throughout, your Lord, spoken to the same one man.

notes.t: Toward your Lord is placed in front of the verb, and in Arabic that inversion carries the sense of only. Not turn to your Lord, but to your Lord and to no one else, turn.
Raghiba is desire that leans toward a thing. With ila it means longing for; with an it means turning away from. The preposition chosen here makes the closing verse a direction given to appetite.
The surah moves from what was done for him, to a rule about hardship, to a command to work, and ends by naming where the wanting should point. Nothing in it is addressed to a crowd.

links.why: the reminders the whole instruction is resting on
sufficient for us is Allah, to Allah we turn in hope, the same verb
